newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK Chief Secretary is public's favourite official.
newsitem.headline: HK Chief Secretary is public's favourite official.

text.p: Anson Chan, who agreed on Saturday to remain under Chinese rule as Hong Kong's top civil servant, would have been the territory's leader if there had been a free vote.

With a radiant smile hiding a tough, no-nonsense core, she has topped popularity polls as the people's favourite to run Hong Kong when more than 150 years of British colonial rule end at midnight on June 30, 1997.
But, sensing she was not Beijing's choice, Chan, 56, did not enter the race for the leadership.

A 400-member Beijing-controlled Selection Committee earlier this month chose shipping tycoon Tung Chee-hwa as the first chief executive for Hong Kong, which will become a Special Administrative Region of China after the handover.
Chan agreed on Saturday to Tung's request that she stay on as Chief Secretary after the handover.
In the latest survey she secured support of 72.7 percent, versus 65.3 percent for Tung, showing that the chief executive designate had failed to eclipse her even after his appointment.
Chan's popularity stems from her proven administrative skills and the people's desire for continuity in the leadership.
Her career has been illuminated by a series of firsts.
After three decades in government service, Chan was appointed Chief Secretary in late 1993 -- the first Chinese and the first woman ever to hold the job.

In that capacity she deputises for colonial Governor Chris Patten, sees to the implementation of government policies and is a senior member in the governor's Executive Council, an advisory cabinet, the highest policy-making body in the territory.

Her job demands political adroitness to prepare the booming capitalist enclave for the embrace of communist-ruled China and to slalom between the conflicting views of Britain, Beijing and Hong Kong. Her performance in the position has left the colony in no doubt about her administrative flair.
Chan was born in Shanghai in 1940, the lunar Year of the Dragon, which Chinese associate with leadership qualities.
While she has to stand by Patten's policies -- which often offend Beijing -- she has made a favourable impression on China.
Last July she met Foreign Minister Qian Qichen and the head of China's Hong Kong and Macau Affairs Office Lu Ping during a visit to Beijing.
Her paternal grandfather, the late General Fang Zhenwu, is considered to have been a great Chinese patriot.

He is reputed to be the man who fired the first shot against the Japanese when they invaded China more than half a century ago. Last August Chan was invited by China's Anhui province to the premiere of a television series about the hero.
Chan's mother achieved fame in China as an artist while her uncle is a highly respected professor of orthopedics.
Before she became Chief Secretary, Chan had been the first woman director of a government department, and then the first female policy secretary.
With Saturday's request from Tung that she stay on, Chan appears not to have harmed her standing with China by her frequent defence of British policies.
Chan has maintained the present legislature should be kept until 1999, contradicting China's plan to dissolve it and appoint a new lawmaking body.
Beijing has vowed to scrap it next July 1 because it was elected under democratic reforms introduced by Patten against Beijing's will.
Chan, the elder of twin girls, moved to Hong Kong with her family from Shanghai in 1948, a year before China's communist takeover, when many Shanghai capitalists poured into the colony.
She graduated from Hong Kong University with a degree in English literature and was later awarded an honorary doctorate by Tufts University of the United States.
